c.tagline: Guinea's humid, chaotic Atlantic capital on a narrow peninsula.

taxi.fareNote: Shared taxis follow fixed per-seat fares along set routes; private/chartered ('dépôt') rides must be negotiated before departure as meters are not used.

emergency.note: Public emergency response is unreliable; most expats use private clinics (e.g., Clinique Pasteur, Ambroise Paré) and arrange own transport.

hood_landmark.Kaloum: Musée National de Guinée, Kaloum, Conakry
hood_landmark.Dixinn: Université Gamal Abdel Nasser de Conakry

avoid.reason: Petty and street crime; caution at night; political demonstrations can turn violent

hood_desc: The government and business core on the tip of the peninsula, walkable, with the main markets, ministries, embassies and the port; convenient but congested and can feel unsafe after dark.
Leafy diplomatic and upscale residential district next to Kaloum with many international hotels, restaurants and the US Embassy area; best for business travelers wanting comfort and security.
A relatively affluent, breezy seaside area popular with NGO workers and expats for its restaurants, supermarkets and calmer residential streets.
A fast-growing residential and commercial suburb further from the center with newer hotels and easier parking, popular for longer stays and conferences.
A quieter, working/middle-class residential neighborhood near the university offering a more local, budget-friendly base with easy taxi access to the center.

water.note: Piped water is often contaminated by leaks and illegal connections; use bottled or treated water.

sys.n: Port Boulbinet ferry to Îles de Los

transit.pay: Cash only in local currency (GNF); shared taxis and buses are paid in cash directly to the driver/conductor, fares are negotiated or fixed by route with no electronic ticketing. Private taxis and ride-hailing (Yango) require price agreement or in-app payment.
transit.hours: Shared taxis and buses run roughly 6am-9pm; limited/no service late at night, private taxis and Yango operate later but with reduced availability and higher risk.
transit.note: Public transport is informal, crowded and often in poor mechanical condition; most visitors rely on hotel-arranged drivers or Yango.

ferry: Port Boulbinet to Îles de Los

tip.r: Not customary but appreciated at hotels/restaurants catering to foreigners; round up taxi fares.

landmarks: Grand Mosque of Conakry (Grande Mosquée Fayçal)
One of the largest mosques in West Africa, its towering twin minarets and gleaming domes dominate the Conakry skyline and draw worshippers and photographers alike.
Palais du Peuple (People's Palace)
This grand Chinese-built congress hall hosts national ceremonies and cultural events, its columned facade and fountains making it a symbol of Guinean sovereignty.
Îles de Los (Los Islands)
A cluster of palm-fringed islands just offshore, once used for slave trading and now a favorite escape for swimming, snorkeling, and picturesque boat trips.
Cathédrale Sainte-Marie de Conakry
The city's striking Catholic cathedral, with its distinctive white towers and colonial-era architecture, stands as a peaceful landmark in the bustling Kaloum district.
National Museum of Guinea
Home to an outstanding collection of traditional masks, statues, and musical instruments, this museum offers a vivid window into Guinea's diverse cultural heritage.
Grand Marché Madina
West Africa's largest and most chaotic market, a sprawling maze of stalls selling everything from fabrics to spices, capturing the raw energy of everyday Conakry life.
Camayenne Botanical Garden
A historic tropical garden established in the colonial era, prized for its shaded avenues, exotic plant collections, and role as a green escape in the capital.
Rogbané Beach
A popular stretch of Atlantic coastline where locals gather at sunset, offering fishermen's pirogues, ocean breezes, and some of the city's best casual photo opportunities.
Stade du 28 Septembre (National Stadium)
Guinea's premier sporting arena and site of historic political rallies, this stadium is a landmark of national pride and the beating heart of local football fandom.
Case d'Olivier de Sanderval
The preserved colonial-era residence of the eccentric French explorer who dreamed of a trans-Saharan railway, offering a quirky glimpse into Conakry's 19th-century history.

train.note: No intercity or international passenger rail. The Conakry Express suburban commuter train on the SBK line has run only intermittently and serves the city corridor, not intercity travel; there is no online booking. The Boke bauxite railway in the north-west (Kamsar-Sangaredi) carries limited company passenger runs, not general travel.

intl.op: buses and shared sept-place taxis from the Madina and Matam garages — no online booking

bus.note: There is no reliable ticketed international coach operator online. Cross-border travel to Bamako (Mali), Dakar (Senegal) and Freetown (Sierra Leone) goes by bus and shared sept-place taxi from the Madina and Matam garages / gare routiere. Carry your passport and Guinean franc / CFA cash for the borders.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferry. Local boats run from Conakry's port out to the Iles de Loos (Kassa, Room) for day trips.
